speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER FOR T1MISKAMING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my painful duty to invite all hon. members to join with me today in paying tribute to the memory of a young man whose death on Friday was profoundly shocking to us. Bruce Lonsdale was one of the most able, most dedicated, and most promising of the younger members of the House of Commons.
Most of us knew him only for a few years, since his election as Member of Parliament for Timiskaming in 1980. In that time we came to understand and share the respect and admiration which led the people of the northern Ontario community of Cobalt to entrust him with great responsibility while he was still in his early twenties. It was because he served so well as town councillor and mayor of Cobalt, especially in the aftermath of the devastating fire which destroyed so much of that community in 1977, that the people of the vast riding of Timiskaming chose him to represent them in Parliament. He repaid their trust by becoming one of the hardest working and most effective Members of Parliament we knew.
His last official act, the announcement in Sturgeon Falls on Friday that the government would open a Statistics Canada office in that community, was typical of the quality of his service. He sought constantly to bring the government closer to the people he represented, and to help create for them new opportunities for employment and fulfilment.
[ Translation]
By the strange irony of fate, Bruce Lonsdale was on his way home after carrying out those official duties when he was killed in a highway accident. I am sure that the members of this House will want to join me in wishing a prompt and complete recovery to the other two who were hurt in this accident. To Mrs. Lonsdale, her children and all Bruce Lonsdale's close relatives, we can only express our sorrow and our sympathy. I would ask you, Madam Speaker, to send them our heartfelt condolences. In Bruce Lonsdale we have lost a friend and a dedicated colleague who was dear to us all and who still had so much to offer Canada and the Canadian people. Although we have witnessed only a short period of his full life, he shall live on in our memory.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER FOR T1MISKAMING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of the official opposition I want to associate us with the words just spoken by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and to express my personal sadness and that of my colleagues on this side of the House at the untimely death last Friday of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Lonsdale).
Many of my colleagues here had the opportunity during Bruce Lonsdale's short period of service in the House of Commons to work very closely with him and he had won, in an uncommonly short time, respect among members on all sides of the House and all parties in this House. As the Prime Minister has said, he was a member here for a very short period of time, but he proved himself during that time to be an able and effective and most energetic representative of all his constituents. He approached his job as Member of Parliament with that same drive and determination that he had exhibited during the period of his service as mayor of Cobalt when he led the citizens of that community in overcoming a great disaster, and he co-ordinated the reconstitution of the town following the fire to which the Prime Minister has referred.
Bruce Lonsdale will be profoundly missed in this House as a member whose standard of service was a model to us all and one who was a very good and personal friend to many of us. We join with all members of the House of Commons in expressing our sympathy to his wife and family.

subtopic: TRIBUTES TO FORMER MEMBER FOR T1MISKAMING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of the members of the New Democratic Party I would like to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) in expressing our deep sympathy to Mr. Lonsdale's wife and children following his tragic death prior to the weekend.
As has been indicated by the Prime Minister, Bruce Lonsdale was a young man, only 32, who had already served the people in his region, first as a mayor and then very diligently here in the House of Commons as a Member of Parliament. It is deeply regretted that any person should lose his or her life in such an accident. It is doubly so for this to happen to one so young who has devoted his energies and talents to the good of his country. It is a sad occasion for us here in the House of Commons. It is a sad event for the people he represented so ably.

Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Whereas interest rates are 3 per cent or 4 per cent higher this year than they were a year ago-and rising again-whereas Agriculture Canada predicts that 1982 net farm incomes will drop 15 per cent this year to a level below that earned in 1974, despite the fact that farm output has more than doubled since that time, and whereas a sound basis for a healthy agricultural economy exists but assistance is needed to help it reach its full potential, I move, seconded by the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish):
That this house calls on the government to introduce legislation to expand the ability of the Farm Credit Corporation to offer low cost credit to farmers, to introduce legislation to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act to offer stabilization based on the real cost of production, and to encourage the establishment of new marketing agencies to provide a defence against low prices.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Statistics Canada recently revealed figures showing that almost one million Canadians are unemployed. That number is rising each week. When you include what are known as the hidden unemployed, those people who consider their employment situation so bleak that they have simply stopped looking, the number of unemployed could easily total a million and a half, which is an estimated 12 per cent of the Canadian labour force.
In light of the fact that the recently tabled federal budget was totally regressive in nature and contained absolutely nothing, either to prevent the escalating losses of existing jobs or to provide for the immediate creation of new ones, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That the November budget of the Minister of Finance, which has been universally condemned by Canadians everywhere, be immediately withdrawn and replaced by a new budget which would realistically address the urgent problems of this nation.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like to speak for a moment of the responsibility of the Minister of Finance. The Canadian Club meets every week.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. We are now in the midst of the deepest depression since the war, having lost
235.000	jobs since August, with lay-offs in the province of Ontario alone, during last month, occurring at the rate of
3.000	per working day.

Madam Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister in his statement about the imposition of martial law in Poland has never condemned that imposition, nor has he recognized any Soviet responsibility for that intervention. The Polish paper Trybuna Ludu, and the U.S.S.R. and Polish media have quoted the Prime Minister for his approval of the repressive actions of the Polish government.
Does the Prime Minister agree with the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs yesterday that the Soviet Union was involved in the military clampdown and has intervened in Polish affairs? If he agrees with him, what changes will now be made in our policy, which to date has
January 25, 1982

supported the Polish and Russian actions in Poland against the Polish people?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: POLAND-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON IMPOSITION OF MARTIAL LAW
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must tell the hon. member that I disagree with his interpretation of our policy, particularly the facts that he set forward. When he says that there was never any condemnation of martial law in Poland, I must point out to him that the very first time I was asked about the imposition of martial law, I believe it was at a press conference on December 19, I regretted the imposition of martial law. 1 went on to indicate that, since it was a fact, we would hope that the military authorities in Poland would permit monitoring by Canada or other people to ensure that the rigours of martial law would be eased as soon as possible. My statement at the year-end went even further along that line.
As to the role of the Soviet Union, I must say that at the time I spoke we had no evidence of any direct intervention by the Soviet Union in Polish affairs. When I say direct, I mean of course beyond the fact that Poland is and has been a satellite of the Soviet Union, as are many other countries in eastern Europe. However, in so far as any direct military intervention is concerned, we had no evidence of that. I understand that some countries claimed to have such evidence. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is in the process of examining and assessing that evidence.

Since the announcement of this unprecedented and reprehensible payment, the Solicitor General has come up with a series of blatantly contradictory statements. One day he said he knew of the payment two days after it was authorized. Later we found out that in fact it was more than two weeks after the payment was authorized. One day he said that the police had a convictable case. Later we learned that in fact they may not have had a convictable case. One day he said there was no federal money. Later-

speechtext:
There were some conflicting statements in the media, and I think all of them have been resolved, or can easily be resolved by some further discussion and further reporting about them.
On the question of conducting an inquiry, this was a matter which was conducted under the provincial policing contract. I have been in touch with the attorney general of the province, to whom the B.C. contingent of the RCMP reports under the provincial policing contract, to ask him if he is satisfied with the way in which the police conducted themselves in that matter. I have been assured that he is. I expect to hear from the Commissioner of the RCMP in the same vein within the next few days, because I have asked him as well to satisfy himself that the policing was properly done in the matter.
If an inquiry is to be conducted into a provincial policing aspect, I do not think the Parliament of Canada should usurp the authority to conduct such an inquiry. It is true that the RCMP is a federal agency, but it is a national police force, and if the Parliament of Canada cannot accept the role it plays in the provinces and cannot allow it to play that role properly so far as the administration of justice is concerned under the attorney general concerned, then we are going to lose the opportunity to use this very important national institution in that way.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO PAYMENT MADE TO CONVICTED MURDERER, CLIFFORD OLSON
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Solicitor General should know very well that not 75 per cent but every penny of the $100,000 paid to Clifford Olson came out of federal coffers, and that alone warrants a federal public independent inquiry.

Madam Speaker, in view of the fact that this payment could establish a very dangerous legal precedent in Canada, and in view of the fact that it is the understanding of federal and provincial authorities that never before has such a payment been made, will the Solicitor General at least give this House the assurance that never again will a payment of such blood money be made under such circumstances and that he will attempt to recover all funds which have been paid so far?

Madam Speaker, in so far as the consideration of where the money came from is concerned, it is true that the federal government is the paymaster of the RCMP, and whether it is for long distance telephone calls, lunches, or gasoline, under the provincial contract the money comes initially from federal coffers. However, I have just negotiated a contract-and I thought the hon. member knew the details of that contract-under which every quarter the federal government claims repayment from the provinces for these outlays on the basis of the federal-provincial cost-sharing agreement, which will change every year over the next ten years in the direction of the federal government contributing a smaller and smaller proportion of that total. I do not think anything turns on the fact that the initial payments are federal, and I think this is simply a red herring being put forward by the hon. member.
In so far as an assurance that such an agreement will never be made again is concerned, I am prepared to assure-as was the case in this case-where an unprecedented type of arrangement is contemplated and demanded by a criminal, that that decision will be raised to the highest level in the province by the RCMP-as was done in this case-that legal advice will be obtained about it, that those politically responsible for the decision will be consulted-as was the case in this case-and that if the decision reached is lawful and if it is consistent with the professional code of the RCMP, it will be their responsibility to make it.

Madam Speaker, this time I must say that I agree with the House leader of the Progressive Conservative Party. A few minutes ago he very aptly pointed out that abuse of this type of question could very easily occur, after the oral question period, if members ask questions ostensibly to inquire about the order of business in the House during the coming days or weeks, and in fact turn them into an opportunity for making political mileage, without the government having a chance to defend itself. I have no secrets about the order of business in the House. The House leaders of the parties meet regularly, and I inform them about the order of business in the House. Questions like those we heard just now may be justified, and basically they are, but they are not appropriate when members put them in this way and at this time of the day, especially when the time of the House is precious.
Now that the economy is going through a very difficult period, and we recognize this, I feel that it is even more important that members on both sides of the House should act responsibly and attend to the business at hand, so that the government can have a debate on the measures it is proposing with a view to fighting inflation and improving social and economic conditions in this country.
In the circumstances, Madam Speaker, I have no intention of letting the time of the House of Commons be wasted in this way. Like the other ministers during question period, I am under no obligation to answer all questions put to me in my capacity of minister.
I shall observe the common courtesy of providing my colleagues with the information they need to plan for the debates in the House. I intend to continue to provide regular information to my fellow House leaders with whom I am on excellent terms. However, should the Progressive Conservative Party decide tomorrow that it is going to follow this example and members from all parts of the country, at least ten, are deployed to ask questions about the business of the House in order to get political points across, I do not think we will ever get around to consideration of individual bills until four o'clock or 4.30 in the afternoon, and I do think Canadians expect more of us than that. The Canadian people are not interested in organized obstruction by the opposition parties and they expect a minimum of co-operation so that we can get on with our work. In the circumstances, I do not intend to provide a specific answer to this question and I would refer the hon. member to his House leader, with whom I shall be glad to discuss the matter.

January 25, 1982
Privilege-Mr. Deans
In any event, according to Beauchesne:
The distinctive mark of a privilege is its ancillary character. The privileges of Parliament are rights which are "absolutely necessary for the due execution of its powers". They are enjoyed by individual Members-
I want to put to Your Honour that a practice has grown up which has eroded my privileges as a member. There is in the land at the moment considerable concern about the economy. It is necessary for me as a member to be able to place before the House of Commons a number of questions directly related to economic matters. It is important that those questions be put in the House of Commons to someone who is held responsible for the administration of matters economic, and at the moment the minister who is primarily responsible for economic matters sits in the other place. There is no parliamentary secretary sitting in the House of Commons who answers directly for the senator who has the primary responsibility for matters of economic direction by the Government of Canada as it relates to industrial development.
I therefore put it to Your Honour that under the interpretations both of Erskine May and of Beauchesne-the interpretation which I just recently placed before you-it is of vital importance that there be an opportunity for members to be able to exercise the privilege which enables them to execute their powers, which I am being denied. subtopic: MR. DEANS-APPOINTMENT OF SENATOR TO CABINET-LACK OF PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
speechtext: I must interrupt the hon. member because I feel that the question he has raised as a question of privilege is not a question of privilege. It has been a practice of this government and of several governments before to appoint ministers who sit in the other House and to designate a minister or ministers who may answer questions members of this House might have concerning the responsibilities of a particular ministry. At any rate, they can be asked of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), should no minister have been designated. The fact that senators sitting in the other House are appointed ministers is a well established practice and, of course, cannot be questioned. Perhaps this is a question concerning the administration of the government, but it cannot be raised as a question of privilege. So I am afraid that the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr Deans) is not founded.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED CRISIS REQUIRING NATIONAL RECOVERY PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the fact that Canada now faces its most severe economic crisis since the Great Depression of the 1930s, with unemployment at a post-war record of 8.6 per cent-in real numbers well over a million Canadians-and inflation at 12.5 per cent, both constituting a national emergency requiring, therefore, an immediate program for national economic recovery with job creation as its highest priority.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLEGED CRISIS REQUIRING NATIONAL RECOVERY PROGRAM
speechtext:
While the Chair recognizes the importance and the seriousness of this matter, the House will agree that the state of the economy has unfortunately been a recurring subject for debate since the beginning of this session and that a change in the figures relating to unemployment and inflation does not necessarily mean that the business of the House should be set aside in order to have an emergency debate.
January 25, 1982

It must also be understood that the Speaker's only duty in this instance-and I hope this is well understood-is to determine whether the request for an immediate debate meets the requirements of Standing Order 26. One such requirement can be found in Subsection (5) of Standing Order 26, where it is stated that the Speaker " ... shall have regard to the probability of the matter being brought before the House within reasonable time by other means".
Let me also quote Citation 287 of Beauchesne's fifth edition:
"Urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but means "urgency of debate", when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the House do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.
The Chair cannot ignore the fact that there will be other opportunities to debate this matter during the current supply period.
Therefore, although the subject matter of this application is of the greatest importance and of concern to all members of the House, because of the continuing nature of the problem and because of the fact that other opportunities will arise to deal with this matter, I cannot accept the hon. member's application for an emergency debate.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as you have indicated, I am rising pursuant to Standing Order 26 regarding a matter that is of the utmost urgency. The situation in Poland continues to be critical. It is not clear if military rule will end within the foreseeable future. Meanwhile, food continues to be in extremely short supply. Large numbers of citizens are imprisoned under inhuman conditions. Despite martial law, the economic crisis is deepening and the possibility of default on loans from western banks, including Canadian banks, continues. Many Polish citizens, particularly sailors, have chosen Canada as a place of refuge. Several western governments have begun to apply sanctions against the Soviet Union and Poland and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) has indicated that Canada is also considering the possibility of sanctions.
Because Canada's attitude to the imposition of military rule has become significant in Poland itself and within the NATO alliance, because sanctions will have an impact on Canada's economy as well as Poland's and because trade and immigration considerations have given Canada an interest in the course of the crisis, I believe the House of Commons should have the opportunity to register its feelings with the government and the people of Poland on behalf of Canada and to urge the Government of Canada to make it clear that Canadians do not approve of the imposition or the course of martial law in Poland.
Motion to Adjourn
If Your Honour finds that the Polish crisis raises important issues in Canada's foreign policy on which the House should be heard, I would move at the appropriate time that the House do now adjourn.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
In this particular case the Standing Order states that the matter must be specific and important, requiring urgent consideration, and indeed the subject of the right hon. member's application meets some of these criteria. Hon. members will recall that the House dealt with this subject last December when two motions were proposed and debated and another motion was adopted by the House.
There is no doubt that the right hon. member raises a very important subject, but I cannot ignore the provisions of Standing Order 26(5) which require me to have regard to the extent to which the matter concerns the administrative responsibility of the government or could come within the scope of ministerial action.
The right hon. member has not made that relationship sufficiently clear for me to conclude that there are grounds for allowing debate under the Standing Order, where a debate might demonstrate that some urgent domestic component would resolve or help resolve the particular crisis in Poland, or the impact that the suggestions made in the course of that debate would have inside Canada.
Undoubtedly there will be other avenues that can be pursued in achieving a debate upon this very important subject. As hon. members are aware, tomorrow has been designated as a supply day and the right hon. member may wish to consider this possibility.
Therefore, with regret, I must decline the right hon. member's application.
Madam Speaker, I move the adjournment of the House.

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
The Department of Veterans Affairs has extensive plans to provide computer systems for regional use. To date, a telecommunications network and inquiry system, linked to a central computer in Ottawa, has been established in all districts and regional offices of the veterans services program.
A new computer system was recently installed in the Pacific region in support of war veterans allowances and civilian war allowances processes. It is planned to extend this and other systems to all regions by the end of the 1982-83 fiscal year.
New systems are also under development to provide support to both field and head office file registry operations. Implementation is planned for the first half of 1982.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-85, to establish a corporation called Canagrex to promote, facilitate and engage in the export of agricultural and food products from Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the Speech from the Throne opening this session of Parliament it was said that food and agriculture were going to be increasingly important to the Canadian economy in the 1980s. That forecast is certainly coming true, probably quicker than many of us realize. Food was a major item on the agenda of the Ottawa Summit last summer, the Commonwealth Conference in Melbourne, and the North-South Conference at Cancun. 1 have personally attended two major world conferences dealing with food recently-the ministerial meeting of the World Food Council in Novi Sad, Yugoslavia, in May, and the biennial conference of the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization in Rome in November.
In one sense the introduction of this legislation into the chamber is the culmination of a dream I have had for a long time. Before coming to the House of Commons, the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) was a strong promoter of such an organization. It is no secret that I have pushed for a Crown corporation to promote agricultural exports at every opportunity. 1 am sure that many other hon. members in the House share that dream, and I am confident that the legislation will not run into any roadblocks along the way. However, in another sense this is just the beginning. Getting Canagrex established and at work on behalf of the Canadian agri-food industry is merely the first step along the road to improving Canada's very important food trade picture. Canada needs such a corporation, and I am convinced that a few years down the road we will look back and wonder how we got along without it for so long.
Canada is a trading nation. Our livelihood depends upon it. That was emphasized in the chamber recently when we passed the Meat Import Act. It is re-emphasized by the enthusiasm of all hon. members every time a new sale of grains or oilseeds is announced. Matters affecting international trade probably take up more time in the House than any other single item.
The importance of trade was stressed in the recent cabinet reorganization announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The fact that all parties co-operated to allow unanimous approval to introduce the Canagrex bill for first reading before Christmas is further evidence of the high priority we all accord to trade policies and programs.
A number of Canadian companies and agencies have worked successfully in the international marketplace; the Canadian Wheat Board and the Canadian Dairy Commission, for example. Several provincial hog boards have moved aggressively in the export field. About 20 per cent of the nation's pork production has been exported in recent years. In 1980 we shipped 166 million pounds of pork to the United States of America and 70.2 million pounds to Japan. Canada was the largest single supplier of pork to Japan in 1980. The Ontario Bean Producers Marketing Board and the British Columbia Tree Fruit Marketing Board are other examples of organizations which have successfully developed export markets. All those agencies and companies which have successfully marketed Canadian agriculture and food products in the past are to be congratulated. They are doing a good job for Canada. Together they exported $7.8 billion worth of products and earned Canada an agricultural trade surplus of $2.7 billion in 1980. The final figures are not in yet, but agricultural exports in 1981 are expected to exceed imports by between $2.5 billion and $2.75 billion. Hardly any other nation in the world can make the claim that it has a net trade balance in food; Canada is one of them.
However, we produce a great variety of food in the country which is not being offered aggressively in the international marketplace. It is fair to say that Canadians still do a better job at production than at sales. When it comes to food that is ready to eat, processed food, as opposed to agricultural products, we are in a trade deficit position of some $300 million. Some people put it much higher, but surely to goodness they do not expect us to produce grapefruit, oranges, bananas, spices, etc.

Manitoba is probably doing better than the hon. member realizes. He probably does not realize what is going on around him. Turning that deficit around is one of the jobs I and many other people who supported the principle of Canagrex see that organization accomplishing. Many of the food manufacturing firms and commodity marketing boards are small and are unfamiliar with the complexities of the international marketplace. For them Canagrex can serve as a source of expert advice. Even more than that, it can become a partner, helping to arrange financing and sharing the risk in joint ventures. In some cases, where opportunity exists and is not being exploited, Canagrex may act on its own to buy and sell agricultural and food products.
Another area where I see Canagrex playing an important role, Mr. Speaker, is in the government to government trade
January 25, 1982

deals which are becoming more and more common, particularly as the Third World and socialist bloc countries become more involved in world trade. Many of those countries handle all their trade through state-trading agencies. They prefer to deal with Canada through a central agency. Even those countries not considered poor, such as the OPEC members, have no hope of being self-sufficient in food in the near future, so they will be in the market for high quality food products for many years to come. They have made no secret about their desire to deal directly with us, and no secret about their unwillingness to deal with some of the huge multinationals.
An example of that occurred last February when Canada signed the $100 million long-term trade deal with Mexico. The state agency handling the sale for Mexico was Conasupo, an agency which has existed for at least ten years, with powers that possibly Canagrex does not have but which were necessary in that country to provide food for about 25 million people in the lower-income or poverty class at reasonable prices. In the future such deals might be handled with Canagrex acting as the umbrella organization for Canadian firms dealing with Conasupo.
Canagrex will have the dual role, Mr. Speaker, of promoting Canadian goods abroad and of promoting within Canada the importance of trade. One problem that Canada has had in the international market is a tendency on the part of some producer organizations to think of export markets as a way of getting rid of surpluses. It is not uncommon to hear it said in government circles and other places that we should perhaps have special legislation just to sell surpluses. However, Mr. Speaker, the one thing we have to remember is that people do not eat just when we have surpluses; they eat 365 days a year. It therefore follows that there should be long-term contracts to guarantee them a steady supply of high quality Canadian food products. I would suggest a minimum term of five years, possibly even longer, ten or 15 years, similar to coal contracts in Alberta or British Columbia. Some of those coal contracts run for 15 years, which is a form of supply-management if I ever saw one. In these contracts their cost increases are guaranteed, and they start negotiating several years before their contracts run out so they can phase out their production. I asked them why they did this and they said that because of the tremendous capital invested they could not operate in any other way.
So, Mr. Speaker, when one measures the tremendous capital the agricultural industry has invested here in Canada, the individual farmer's investment in land and equipment, it is obvious that the investment has to be utilized.
As I said earlier here today, agriculture with its associated industries is the biggest employer in Canada. Let no one forget that: the biggest single employer. What we are saying with Canagrex is that we can make it an even bigger and more important one. Canada would not be able to establish, for instance, the kind of market we want if we are just going to sell when we have surpluses. I have seen it so often, as a minister, as a backbencher and before that in farm organiza-
Canagrex Act
tions when everyone was striving to make a fast buck with a quick sale of a surplus product somewhere in the world. We have looked for an export market when we had a surplus to dispose of, and ignored it when the domestic market was large enough to handle all our production.
Canada will not be able to establish itself as a serious trading nation with such an attitude. Countries interested in buying Canadian produce will be looking for continuity of supply and that is what we want, because it will mean Canadian producers will have a steady market and a steady income, which is what most of the farmers that I talk to want. I know that if we offer that kind of incentive to the farmers, all you will have to do, Mr. Speaker, is just watch them go.
As I said last February when the cabinet first gave approval to the idea of Canagrex, the agency's job will be to increase the volume and variety of sales of Canadian agricultural and food products. That will mean increased income for farmers and a shot in the arm for the whole economy. It will not be wasting time as we have done in the House today, because Canagrex cannot work if we are going to have that kind of operation.

Agricultural exports are vital to the prosperity of the Canadian food and agriculture sector. Traditionally, agricultural exports have made up 40 to 45 per cent of farm cash receipts. Practically no other country is as dependent on exports as we are.
Canagrex will help to expand Canadian food production and processing, and this will provide many new jobs in an industry which is already one of the nation's largest employers, if not the largest.
As you can see from the legislation, Canagrex will run a tight ship. It will not be a big bureaucracy, as some people have suggested. It will be run by a board of 11 directors reporting to the Minister of Agriculture, seven of whom will be appointed from outside the federal public service, and they will be well qualified to deal in agricultural trade matters.
There will also be a policy advisory committee made up of representatives from provincial governments, the business community and farm organizations which will advise me on all matters associated with market development strategy. The working officers will be a president and two vice-presidents who will be hired to administer Canagrex under the direction of the board of directors.
Hon. members will recognize that to be fully effective and to achieve its objection of reinforcing the export capabilities of the food and agricultural sector, the corporation must have wide-ranging powers. These include the ability to make contracts, enter into joint ventures, provide grants and contributions, give loans and guarantees, hold property and, if necessary, purchase, process, package and export food products. It will be able to charge for its services, and the projects it undertakes are expected to be economically viable.

January 25, 1982
Canagrex Act
The bill also provides for Canagrex to be funded annually from money appropriated by Parliament. It will not engage in paying direct subsidies on a product to either producers or processors, nor will it deal in products under the control of the Canadian Wheat Board or the Canadian Dairy Commission unless it is invited to do so. In that way, Mr. Speaker, it will not duplicate the efforts of other Crown agencies.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. It being six o'clock, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock this evening.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

As I was saying when we adjourned at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, Canagrex must have wide-ranging powers to enable it to do the job we want it to do. That includes the ability to make contracts, enter into joint ventures, provide grants and contributions, give loans and guarantees, hold property and, if necessary, purchase, process, package and export food products. Canagrex will be able to charge for its services, and the projects it will undertake are expected to be economically viable.
The bill also provides for Canagrex to be funded annually from money appropriated by Parliament. It will not engage in paying direct subsidies on a product to either producers or processors, nor will it deal in products under the control of the Canadian Wheat Board or the Canadian Dairy Commission unless invited to do so. That is to avoid duplication of the efforts of other Crown agencies.
Canagrex will co-operate with and use existing programs and activities of the federal government wherever appropriate. I will report annually to Parliament on the operations of Canagrex and will table a summary of its annual capital budget.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, breaks new ground in that it requires the management of Canagrex to prepare annually a three-year corporate plan spelling out its proposed activities.
I have spent a lot of time, Mr. Speaker, these past few months discussing with the agriculture and food sector a long-term strategy for the development of an agri-food industry that will keep Canada in the lead in this industry for the remainder of this century. It is an exciting prospect, one which has generated a lot of interest among all sectors of the industry in Canada, from primary producer to consumer.
From the very beginning I have emphasized-and the agrifood strategy document, "Challenge for Growth", repeats this-that market development is the spark which will give life to the strategy. It must be clear to everyone that production
without a market is not only a waste of food but is an invitation to financial ruin for the producer.
We cannot just produce and pile it up and hope to God that someone is going to buy it at a fair price. Too often in the past we have seen farmers produce a big crop of an excellent quality product, whether it be from the fields or in the livestock industry, only to sell it in the world market below the cost of production. That is what is happening in the red meat industry in Canada today. Some of this product is going to countries which can well afford to pay a decent price, countries such as the United States of America and Japan. Some of it is going to other countries such as the U.S.S.R. where they can send people into space but cannot feed themselves. There is no reason in the world why we should subsidize them simply because we are efficient and produce surplus only to sell it into their markets below the cost of production. 1 sometimes wonder why farmers would ever want to produce anything under those circumstances.
So, Mr. Speaker, Canagrex is a very important part of the agri-food strategy because it is one of the ways by which we will achieve market development on which the industry's future depends. In fact, I am convinced we will not be able to open up the necessary markets for food which Canada is ideally situated to supply unless we have a Crown corporation such as Canagrex to represent Canada in the world market place.
I know I can count on the support of this chamber to give swift approval to this bill so that we can take this next important step in the development of the agriculture and food industry. I know I can count on members of the opposition to make short, precise and constructive speeches. Perhaps we can even pass the bill in its entirety this evening, give it second and third reading, and away we go! We can have it in operation, and our farmers could be signing contracts before spring begins.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome this opportunity to enter the debate this evening following the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I welcome the opportunity to make some comments on Bill C-85 which, of course, establishes the Crown corporation of Canagrex. I welcome it because it is at least an indication that this government at long last is showing some interest, for the time being, in the promotion of agriculture or the sale of agricultural products. I wonder why it took some ten months, from February to December, to prepare this legislation when farm organizations and farm leaders have been requesting this type of scheme for at least five or six years. I can recall my first introduction to the Canagrex concept when it was brought to the attention of our caucus back in 1973. The minister may doubt this, but it was brought to our attention back in 1973 by my colleague, the hon. member who still represents the riding of Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton).
January 25, 1982

However, as we are aware, on February 20, 1981, nearly a year ago, the Minister of Agriculture announced that the cabinet had given approval for the establishment of the agriculture export corporation, Canagrex. As the minister said, "Cabinet has given the green light for the creation of Canagrex". It was announced on February 20, 1981. If it took ten months for the green light, then it is no wonder that the workings of this government have been compared to a traffic jam, because we know that there is a great deal of commotion and a great deal of horn sounding in a traffic jam, but there is virtually little or no forward movement. However, this is really the history and the record of this government, particularly when it comes to dealing with the agricultural industry, which is the most important and most vital industry not only in Canada but of course in other countries as well.
It should also be noted that even the February 20 announcement came one year after the 1980 election, and in that campaign Canagrex formed a very integral and important part of the Liberal Party's agricultural platform. If this government had acted upon this promise a year and a half ago and had given priority to increasing agricultural exports, then our agricultural industry might not be experiencing the same severe economic distress which plagues it today.
The rationale given for Canagrex is that many of Canada's smaller agri-businesses and farm organizations lack the expertise, knowledge and indeed the financial resources to be aggressive and effective as export marketers. Canagrex would, therefore, become directly involved in joint ventures with agricultural exporters by providing loans and guarantees.
Certainly, priority must be given to increasing our agricultural exports. I am sure the minister is very much aware of this. Although Canada has traditionally had a food trade surplus, this surplus has largely been an illusion. It is dependent on the variations of the world grain market and the world grain trade. However, when grain sales are removed or omitted from our agricultural trade calculations, we find that Canada has been suffering from an even worsening food trade deficit. This deficit has increased from an average of about $449 billion some 12 years ago in 1970, to a deficit of $1.9 billion in 1979.
We must work very hard and diligently to reduce this deficit. Increasing our agricultural exports, of course, is one way; decreasing our imports of food which can be successfully and economically grown here in Canada is naturally another. It is estimated that Canada imports about $3 billion worth of agricultural products which could be grown here in Canada, products such as apples, fresh vegetables, oil seeds, soybeans, and oats for milling and breakfast cereal, to name but a few. The government must develop new policies which will encourage import replacement.
I know that there are a great many pros and cons to an agricultural export corporation. I am anxious that the merits of Canagrex be fully discussed in committee. In committee and indeed during debate in the House, my colleagues and I will try to find out whether Canagrex is the best method of increasing our agricultural exports.
Canagrex Act
One of the major problems facing Canagrex will be its effectiveness in views of its very limited budget and staff. In his original proposal, the Minister of Agriculture set out what he thought should be the minimum standards of Canagrex. These minimum standards consisted of a budget of $62.3 million and a staff of between 125 and 175 people. These figures were taken from the minister's announcement. I would say that today we are a little short on funds and long on staff. However, as with so many of the minister's proposals, he failed to manoeuvre these minimum standards which he had established on February 20, 1981, through cabinet. In his February 20 statement, the minister reported that cabinet had approved a budget for Canagrex, not one of $62 million but rather one of $12.3 million, that is $50 million less than what the minister thought was necessary, and that this money had to be spread over a period of three years. Therefore, on an annual basis for the next three years, provided the bill receives approval, the corporation will receive a budget, not of $62.3 million but rather of $4.1 million.
Concerning staffing, the cabinet approved a staff of 12. Again that amounts to 163 people fewer than what the minister set out in his minimum standards. I suppose that if we wanted to be critical of the minister and, after all, he is the Minister of Agriculture and must assume and accept the responsibilities, we could say that at least the minister continues to be successful at failing to get whatever measures he wants through the cabinet intact.
However, with these massive reductions from the minister's own personal assessment of minimum standards for Canagrex, I wonder whether the corporation will be able to perform adequately the role laid out for it in Bill C-85. Again, in committee, my colleagues and I will want to know whether Canagrex might not serve a more useful purpose by being part of the minister's own department, by being a division within Agriculture Canada, rather than another Crown corporation. I do not know. I suppose it would be a fair question to ask the minister if he could tell me now just how many Crown corporations are owned by the government. I know there has been some difficulty in the past with one minister saying there are 185 Crown corporations and someone else contradicting him. If Canagrex receives approval, I just wonder how many Crown corporations will fall under the jurisdiction of the government.
We will also want to be very careful that Canagrex does not repeat the marketing miscalculations of the Canadian Dairy Commission, because David Kates, the deputy chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, and Mr. Justice Hugh Gibson of the federal court of Canada have found, in two separate reports, that there is almost no limit to the potential for ill-advised government intervention for which there is practically no mechanism for accountability. That is a pretty damning statement. The Canadian Dairy Commission has done an excellent job for producers and consumers over the years and has been very effective in the export market field. These revelations could hardly come at a worse time. With the federal government's dairy policy review hanging over the

January 25, 1982
Canagrex Act
heads of Canadian dairy farmers, it could add powerful ammunition to those people in the bureaucracy and those in Treasury Board. Because of the delay, I am convinced there must be some reluctance on the part of some cabinet colleagues of the Minister of Agriculture. They must be opposing the national dairy policy. We have to see what cabinet did to the Canagrex budget and staff. If this same mentality or feeling applies, I hate to think what it could do to the national dairy policy.
If Canagrex is to be enacted, we have to make sure the government has learned from its mistakes. Bill C-85 must not contain provisions which will allow for the abuse of intervention and the abuse of power.
There are other questions regarding Canagrex which have to be answered. It is appropriate that a number of questions be raised, questions such as the role of Canagrex in the Canadian export business. Will it act in support of or in competition with existing Canadian exporters? There will be the determination of how to allocate a sale. If a market is found for a particular commodity or product, who determines the sale and which company or farm group is given the opportunity to supply the goods?
How do we ensure the board of directors of Canagrex is composed of qualified people? These people are not around the country in great numbers. It is extremely important that we secure well-qualified people, people who are ready to work and are capable of taking appropriate action, and not just create another government body which the government can utilize as an opportunity to pass out some political patronage.

The reporting relationship with Agriculture Canada is extremely important. As I indicated earlier, our concept of Canagrex is that it would not necessarily be a Crown corporation, although there may be some problems associated with that.
There is also the reporting relationship with Industry, Trade and Commerce. I could probably add External Affairs when we are dealing in the export market. Canagrex will have a very limited staff. Therefore, co-operation among these three departments will be extremely important.
Canagrex will by necessity be dependent upon the co-operation of these three departments. As a result, we must examine the willingness of these departments to co-operate and share their resources with Canagrex. The minister did not indicate this, but perhaps others who follow him will. I understand a number of his colleagues want to comment on Canagrex. Perhaps they will answer the question of how it will fit in with the latest reorganization that has taken place between Industry, Trade and Commerce and External Affairs.
There is also the question of whether there ought to be a separate Crown corpporation to look after agricultural exports or whether this body, as I indicated, might well do the job
being a branch or division within the minister's department, Agriculture Canada.
I would have thought the government might have tried to improve other more basic needs of agricultural exports in the absence of the corporation. One of these basic needs, of course, is the dissemination of information and material. It has always amazed me that a country such as Canada which has 115 embassies and trade offices or consulates abroad has an agriculturalist specialist on staff in only ten. Of these ten, only one is in a Third World country, India, despite the fact that in 1980 nearly 25 per cent of our agricultural exports went to the Third World.
Because of the low representation abroad, Canadian exporters have suffered when it came to finding and defining export opportunities. It is extremely difficult for a person not completely familiar with the fundamentals of agriculture to assess the agricultural needs of a foreign country and to be aware of whether Canadian firms can supply these services or products.
The government can also encourage exporters through information availability. I am aware that Agriculture Canada has sponsored several seminars for agricultural exporters, people in the agri-food industry, and the bankers. These seminars should provide an opportunity for exporters to learn more about sources of financing, export credit, insurance services and market information.
I hope the minister will make certain that these export seminars continue, that they will involve a broad cross-section of agricultural producers and that they will be held in all regions of this country.
I hope that Bill C-85 does not mark the end of this government's attention to agriculture. It has always seemed that this government can only find the time to deal with one major agricultural bill per year. Last year, 1981, it was the meat import law. This year, 1982, it is Canagrex. Canadian agriculture deserves better priority and attention than it has received from this government. The agricultural industry is suffering deeply as a result of this government's high interest rate policy. The latest is the devastating budget that the minister's colleague brought forward on November 12 which adversely affects farmers.
Where are the government measures designed to deal with this economic crisis? Where is the long-promised legislation which would allow the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow supplementary funds from the private marketplace? The Minister of Agriculture has been promising such legislation for over a year. I am being fairly complimentary when I say a year. On second thought, it might be as many as five years.
If such legislation had been enacted last year or a couple of years ago, many Canadian farmers might still be in business today. Last year, 261 farmers declared bankruptcy. Untold hundreds more were forced out of business through foreclosures and forced sales. These heavy losses are a real threat to our future food security. The government should be doing its utmost to reverse this very serious trend.
January 25, 1982

Unfortunately, the government has done virtually nothing. In fact, it has helped to make matters worse by bringing down one of the most disastrous budgets on record. The budget and its many changes have again demonstrated that this government simply does not know what it is doing. On the one hand there is the Minister of Agriculture encouraging farmers to stay in business for the good of Canada and Canadians. On the other hand, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) which penalizes very seriously the retirement income of farmers who have worked a lifetime providing the food requirements for Canadians and many other hundreds of thousands of people beyond our borders. The Minister of Finance brought in a budget making unfair tax changes to the income-averaging annuity contracts and to the capital gains tax reserves. Also, the Minister of Agriculture, prior to the budget, kept telling farm group after farm group that meaningful economic assistance would be forthcoming in the budget.
Does the minister actually believe that an extra $50 million in the Farm Credit Corporation is really of assistance, especially when the estimates of the basic need for the Farm Credit Corporation has been calculated to be between $500 million and $1 billion? In fact, $45 million of that $50 million will be paid back fully in principal and interest. Does the minister actually believe that the cancellation of the Small Business Development Bond Program at the end of this year, except for those in dire straits, is beneficial to Canadian agriculture? I would hope not.
It is obvious that the minister does not understand the financial crisis facing Canadian agriculture today. He obviously does not have the necessary input and clout and influence in cabinet to secure the necessary programs and policies to cope with the current situation in the agricultural industry today. Rather than dealing with a piece of legislation which would offer immediate help and hope to Canadian farmers, we are dealing with legislation creating a new Crown corporation, a corporation which in the short term will benefit mainly its chairman in the form of a suggested salary of between $100,000 and $200,000. However, the long-term benefits will not accrue to farmers until several years later.
I heard the minister make a comment on that, but these are the rumours and I raise them. I am sure that other speakers will raise them.
Grocery product manufacturers pay their manager $120,000.

Therefore, we should be dealing with legislation which will help Canadian agriculture immediately. There should be legislation for an immediate moratorium on farm bankruptcies, foreclosures and forced sales, in order to prevent 48-hour auction sales, to stop the sale of productive assets, to eliminate the sale of valuable livestock at slaughterhouse prices and to give the necessary time for governments to put into place effective and meaningful programs and policies for the survival and indeed for the recovery of the agricultural
Canagrex Act
industry. We should be amending the Farm Credit Corporation legislation so as to allow it to borrow funds from the private marketplace.

I think it is very obvious.
Rather than the tax disincentives in the budget, the Minister of Agriculture should have been able to convince his colleague, the Minister of Finance, to implement the agri-bound concept. This would give farmers access to money at interest rates below prime. The cost to the public treasury would be extremely small and the benefits to the farm community would be immense.
Understandably, the farm community today is absolutely convinced that this government does not care about the agricultural industry. Not only does the agricultural industry need adequate financial support today, it also needs support through a meaningful piece of legislation. The Minister of Agriculture would certainly do well to give serious consideration to the proposal of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture to set up a market risk insurance plan which would involve a three-way participation among the two levels of government and the producer.
Another area which could be dealt with would be an upgrading of the V-day values for the capital gains tax. The minister should be familiar with this suggestion because this has been a long-time election promise by his government, a promise which is always ignored shortly after the election campaign is over.
The minister has promised time and time again to the agricultural community to update the valuation day values of the present day from 1971 to 1974 values. I suggest that a far better solution to deal with capital gains would be a once-in-a-lifetime exemption from the sale of a farm by a bona fide farmer.
We could also be dealing with legislation with respect to rebates on fuels used for food production. Given the increases in the energy prices, a total exemption of tax would be appropriate and would indeed benefit all segments of the agri-food industry. Producers, processors, distributors and indeed 24 million Canadians would benefit from that type of legislation.
It is interesting to note that the price of gasoline has increased by approximately 75 cents a gallon since we received the message that, upon election, the government would keep fuel prices down. Of that 75 cents, 36 cents is taken out in tax alone, which works out to about twice as much as 18 cents.
Measures could be implemented to help market returns, because many of today's producers are suffering from a severe cost price squeeze. At the same time, because of the lack of advertising, promotion and public information, many Canadian consumers are willing to pay about $1.50 for a head of

January 25, 1982
Canagrex Act
grade D imported lettuce. Surely these consumers would be willing to pay a little more for a grade A Canadian product. However, because of the twisted priorities of this government, we do not have any of these worth-while measures to deal with. We can only debate the merits of Canagrex, another Crown corporation to which it is rumoured the present Minister of Agriculture might be heading once it is established. If that rumour is true, Mr. Speaker, I can understand why so many people are so eager to have this legislation passed so quickly. Maybe there is another thought in the back of the minister's mind to account for the fact that he is extremely anxious that this bill actually pass tonight and not on Wednesday.
1 might even be thinking about giving you a job.

I appreciate the minister's comment. However, there are other questions which we will be asking throughout the debate and more particularly throughout the committee stage. We want to be assured of accountability and control. We want to have some indication as to the possible intentions the government might have with regard to who might serve on the board of directors, whom they might have in mind to take on the position of president and chairman.
We want to discuss to some degree the salaries, expenses and superannuation and we would be quite willing to talk about some of these issues in an in camera session of the standing committee. It is possible because it has been done before with regard to the beef import law. I think we achieved some measure of success because of the fact that there was an offer and a willingness on the part of the minister to convey some of this information to us in an in camera session.
The minister has indicated that he would be making a report to Parliament on the progress of Canagrex. That is fine, but it is really not good enough. We would like to see the minister not only table the report from Canagrex on an annual basis but have the report automatically referred to committee. If Canagrex is formed, we are anxious to see it operate successfully and to ensure that it does indeed increase the export sale of Canadian agricultural products. However, if it does not perform adequately, we want to know about it. We can only know about it if the annual report is referred to committee, thus allowing us to cross examine the officials of Canagrex during committee hearings.
We would also like to see a sunset clause provided in this legislation which would allow a Crown corporation to receive a mandate for a further five years if it is doing an effective job. I believe there are some 200 Crown corporations in Canada, many of which could be wound down. It would be no loss to the Canadian taxpayer, and in fact it would probably be a tax saving.
As I have indicated, the message is that we certainly accept the concept of conditional or qualified support. I have raised some questions. Others will be raised by my colleagues in the debate. Yet other questions will be put forward in committee, and the government must be able to provide answers to those questions and must be able to convince the members of the
committee of the necessity of a separate Crown corporation to support agricultural products.
I will just close my remarks by saying that if this can be done and if it is not possible to perform this function having Canagrex as a division within Agriculture Canada or within the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce-I am interested only in increasing export sales-and if we can be satisfied about some other matters which will be raised, I am certain Canagrex will receive some support.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on this particular piece of legislation. It has been a long time since it was announced. We in this corner of the House are basically optimistic about the legislation in the same way, I suppose, farmers are optimistic when they go out to seed new crops. We do not see very much description as to what will be brought about here, but we think that the concept and the idea has some possibilities. We do, however, have a number of questions, and we will be raising them in the next few days and in committee.
The farm community too has waited a long time for this legislation. The minister has talked about it and talked about it. It was announced back in February of last year. The bill was finally printed and before us just a few weeks before this session was interrupted for the Christmas break. We appreciate the minister's comments in his speech this evening pleading for speedy passage, but given the fact that this has been coming for lo this past year at least and being cognizant of the remarks of the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), who pointed out that this legislation has had a much longer gestation period even than that, I think a few more days of careful discussion and consideration can help rather than hinder the plan behind this legislation.
We agree that there are special needs for some agricultural exports which will require the full-time attention and practical knowledge of people involved in the process at all times. My limited experience in the marketing of agricultural products with the Saskatchewan Hog Marketing Commission and the Canadian Wheat Board advisory committee tells me that this is a very important role, and it is very important that it be fullfilled correctly and properly. I do not agree with some critics of this type of marketing that it cannot play a useful role.
I have some questions about the functions of Canagrex which I will be raising here and in the committee, but the concept itself is one which deserves further attention and deserves developing.
I realize that some people in the industry think that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce should be carrying out these kinds of duties through its commercial counsellors, and indeed some of the job of selling Canadian agricultural products can be carried out that way-and is- but during the Christmas break the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce underwent a revamping. There is a not

too well understood combining of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce with foreign affairs postings. This probably leaves even more room for Canagrex to function on the world stage, with the assistance and full co-operation of commercial counsellors in Canadian embassies and trade offices.
We do see that there will be some difficulties for Canagrex, If I were to make a short list of the kinds of products Canagrex is likely to be handling-products which have a potential for further exports-a short list not ranked by priority or anything, it would include pork, potatoes, higher grade beef cuts-a form of boxed beef-specialized products such as lentils, fababeans, mustard, fescue for grass seed, fresh peas, fresh beans, dried peas, dried beans and other vegetables for the frozen trade. In particular, root vegetables are something we produce quite competitively. Also, we see some possibilities for apples and apple products, and given some slight change in the world economic climate, we think there is a potential for poultry products, including chicks and breeding stock, as well as some opportunity for increases in semen sales.
When we look at that list, the job Canagrex has outlined for itself, the budget it has to operate under and the guidelines which are probable and likely, we conclude that Canagrex's first job is-perhaps unfortunately-likely to be to plump for the development of some of these smaller volume products. I say that from my limited experience with pork producers, for instance, which I think some of the drafters of Canagrex had hoped would be one of its first customers, there are some problems to overcome with the marketing of pork which perhaps some of the weaker, less developed commodities will not have, simply because their producers have not been established long enough to develop them. Pork producers have developed a series of marketing agencies in the provinces. In addition to that, all of the packing houses in this country have very sizeable pork departments, and they strive to export pork. In short, when export buyers are interested in Canadian pork or show some interest in Canadian pork, there is a multitude of potential sellers knocking at their door attempting to sell them that commodity. In an ideal world, if we could go to those countries with just one agency-one seller-it would be to the advantage of Canadian producers, Canadian processors and the whole pork industry. However, in the competitive climate we have set up in this country, that will be very, very difficult to carry out. The directors, managing directors and the chief executive officer of Canagrex will not only have to be very good salesmen and know the international market, but the organization will also have to have an ability to bring together the various sectors, organizations and groups within the country if they are to be able to guarantee a product.
I think that is one of the basic problems Canagrex will have. It may be successful in bringing together a group of people who are very good at exporting and making contacts in the export trade for agricultural products, but the back-up-the integrated production to consumer chain of command, so to speak-which is there in some of the one-desk selling agencies such as the Canadian Wheat Board and the Canadian Dairy Commission will be lacking in Canagrex. I think this is one of
Canagrex Act
its shortcomings, by virtue of the fact that it is a voluntary organization and will be able to function only as well as its ability to bring the various sectors of the industry together.
I think we should take a moment or two to analyse how difficult this job will be and the position that Canagrex will find itself in. How is a brand new organization to break into, say, the Japanese market for pork almost overnight when we already have eight or nine in total, and certainly four or five, very large meat processing companies attempting, and some succeeding, to break into that market every month of the year? Are those processing plants going to give up their access to the Japanese market and stand aside for Canagrex? I doubt that, Mr. Speaker. They do not stand aside for some pork marketing boards in this country or for anyone else. In the process of trying to break into the market, will Canagrex not have to do the same thing as some provincial boards and some processing plants have had to do, that is, offer a better deal, a lower price and, we hope, a better product? How are they to do that and still bring benefit to Canadian producers? That is a conundrum that will have to be solved in the agricultural committee. I think it should be solved before Canagrex is struck.
I realize that the 11 board members set their own terms of reference, so to speak, and set their own marketing program on a three-year basis, but there must be some kind of guideline if they are to do an intelligent job. I do not see any immediate advantage unless further back-up is provided and further assistance is granted to help them break into the larger markets with commodities such as pork. That is too bad, Mr. Speaker. It is my understanding that one of the trump cards for touting Canagrex in this country is to help sell important products like pork. As I understand this legislation, that is not likely to happen.
We know from the description of Canagrex that was presented by the minister and from papers which were introduced prior to the presentation of Canagrex in the form of a bill, that it is supposed to have the power to intervene in the market where needed or desired in order to purchase, process or sell products. I congratulate the minister and the government for leaving these powers in the bill in face of the criticisms made by the Canadian meat council, as I believe it is called. The government and members of the House, however, should be conscious of the fact that the ability to intervene at any stage and make purchases at any stage in the production through processing, still means that it has to be done in competition with the processors and, in some cases, with the marketing boards. It will sometimes be very difficult for the producers to see that they have gained any advantage, because in order to compete they will probably be bidding the price down rather than raising it and thus ensuring that the total efforts of the industry are consolidated, which I think was the intention in the first place.

How is competition going to lower the price?

January 25, 1982
Canagrex Act

My friend asks how competition is going to lower the price. Competition always lowers the price in an export market when the buyer is able to shop around. If pork is available from eight or ten different sources, the Japanese will buy it from the cheapest source. Those who have supplied the Japanese in the past will have to be able to buy at a price that will allow them to continue to supply that market. Eventually the price has to be bid down to the producer in order to meet the price constraints of the world market.
I think there are very definite price constraints in the world market. There are not many countries that are able and willing to pay the price for products that will result in a modest profit to the Canadian producer. That is one of the problems this particular strategy has not addressed very well. That, at least, makes it consistent with the agri-food policy because I am not sure that the farm sector has been addressed very well in the agri-food policy being presented to the country by the government and the Department of Agriculture.
The quality of this agency will depend on the quality of the people attracted or appointed to it. If a raft of political appointees or a bunch of burned out civil servants who are looking for close to retirement sinecures are appointed, then Canagrex will not be very effective. It will quickly fade into obscurity and there will be no benefit derived at the farm level or in world trade. If dynamic and imaginative people are appointed who are prepared to look at the industry with an open mind and a pragmatic philosophy toward marketing, then Canagrex can succeed.
I cannot allow this debate to go too much further without mentioning one other concern that I have and that is how inappropriate it is for an agency like Canagrex to be marketing in Third World countries. In the past we have had some rather unfortunate examples of Canadian agricultural agencies and aid agencies providing products to Third World countries which have no way of using them. We have given skim milk powder and milk products to countries whose people have not consumed milk since the time they were weaned. They have never developed the ability to digest milk and they do not have the appropriate enzymes in their stomachs to aid in the digestion of dairy products.
We have made gifts and have provided aid for the purchase of commodities in countries which simply do not have a societal acceptance of such commodities. While some terrible mistakes have been made in the past, I think this should not hinder us from attempting to aid countries where the industrial process is advanced enough that new forms of food will be welcomed. We should make certain, however, that Canagrex is made aware of some of the gaffes that Canada made in Third World countries in the past and that these are not repeated.
Canagrex is a good idea, Mr. Speaker. But some of the conditions necessary to make it a success are not present in Canada at the moment and they are not within the scope of Canagrex itself. I think particularly of the ability to provide the back-up for the marketing thrust. When the minister spoke, he said that you cannot have production without a market because this means waste, but then a little later he said
that Canada is so efficient that it produces surpluses. There seems to be a contradiction in terms in these remarks. If we are truly efficient in our marketing process and the control of production, we should be able to avoid surpluses.
I hope we do not set up an agency which is not cognizant of our ability to produce and the cost of that production. This is fundamental and almost simplistic, but our agricultural policy over the past few years seems to have missed those fundamentals. The agri-food strategy presented to us over the last several months appears not to pay much attention to the basic production unit. For instance, if we are to have truly efficient agriculture in the country, one would think that our agriculture, as opposed to that of countries with inefficient agriculture, would be able to generate adequate investment capital to keep itself going and growing. This has not been the case in Canadian agriculture, basically because farm prices are such that net incomes have not grown as Canadian agriculture has grown. In 1974, realized net incomes in the country were $3.5 billion, a fairly hefty sum, but through all the years from 1974 to 1980-81, it has not risen much above that amount. We have hung in there around $3.5 billion of net income. In fact, the projected outlook for 1982 is that it will be 15 per cent lower or slightly lower than $3.5 billion. For seven or eight years, net incomes have been virtually the same as they were back in 1974, in spite of the fact that a 1974 dollar buys just about twice what a 1981 or 1982 dollar buys. In real terms, net farm incomes have been cut in half. This was not from the lack of production. Production in dollar terms rose 2.5 times during that period of time.
How did farmers continue to stay in business? They did it by adding to their farm debt. They went into the period of time which I have been discussing with just under $7 billion worth of debt, and by the end of 1980 the most recent figures I have been able to obtain indicate a debt of $16.5 billion. Up to the present time, we have accumulated an extra debt of $10 billion to $12 billion because of a lack of ability to create adequate farm incomes in order to provide reinvestment on farms. It is not a particularly healthy industry from which to sell more product, but it is an integrated part of the system and must be acted upon. I do not think adequate attention has been paid to basic producers or farmers down on the land. What benefit will they receive from Canagrex? If it does not show up in improved net incomes, why should they care or become involved? Why should their little marketing boards, marketing co-ops or community organizations ask Canagrex to sell their products for them? This must be considered as part of the agri-food strategy, but I do not think it is being considered in the current one before us at this time.
Interest rates are rising. Over the period of time about which I have been talking, interest costs to Canadian farmers rose from $473 million to approximately $2.2 billion at the end of 1981. This one little part of agricultural production costs has risen five times at the same time as net farm incomes have remained the same. One could refer to many more input costs of farmers which have climbed, but interest rates have climbed

phenomenally. It is part of the agri-food strategy and the agri-food chain which is not being addressed by the government. It must be tackled if Canagrex is to be a success.
