Another aspect of the agri-food policy which can affect the success or failure of Canagrex is the transportation policy. The country has grown to the extent it has, in terms of the agricultural output, because of an agricultural transportation policy which takes care of outside regions. It was designed to encourage the production of prairie grain and the movement of products at reduced rates to the maritimes. It is an integral part of the Canadian agricultural policy structure, a part which should not be changed rapidly or in haste for reasons which have nothing to do with agricultural productivity. We do not see how increasing the so-called Crow rate on grains will do anything for Canadian agriculture. We do not see how the reduction of net incomes by transferring money from the pockets of farmers to the pockets of the railways will do anything for the redevelopment or continued development of agriculture, an industry which already borrows heavily to keep its investment capital in shape. We do not think it is a wise trade-off to be made or even to be proposed, yet we are faced with rumours of this and speeches by cabinet ministers that this is about to happen.
The transportation policy does not take into account processed goods from certain regions. For instance, processed chilled beef can be shipped from Toronto to Saskatoon, if anyone wants to ship it in that direction, for much less than it can be shipped from Saskatoon to Toronto. It is not regulated, it is not statutory. It is not in existence because of some ancient agreement with the CPR so that it could develop a rail line into Trail to develop some mines. It is just there because it is the manner in which railways priced their products. That pricing structure probably has more to do with the location of packing plants than has the Crow rate, yet we in the House are not attacking or addressing this in public very much.
We do not hear of it very much.

Canagrex will have to be assisted by policies which handle the transportation problem as well as the farm pricing problem. The question of market stabilization is not very well explained in the bill. The bill makes clear those things with which Canagrex will not involve itself. Clause 14(2)(a) indicates that Canagrex shall not "pay to producers or processors a subsidy directly on any Canadian agricultural product or food product", yet we do not have completely adequate stabilization programs so that price guarantees are built into the production formula for farmers. If the farmers are not certain of some price guarantees, why would they produce products for Canagrex to market? They will not do it only because Canagrex is there. There must be an advantage at the farm. That has not been made clear in this bill up to this point, in part because there are not clearly stated policies for transportation and income protection.
Canagrex Act
I think this bill ought to be dealt with in committee. There are a great many aspects of the bill to which we should have answers before it is passed in the House. The question of auditing has not made that clear. It says that the Auditor General shall audit the books. It does not spell out all of the guidelines in that regard. It still leaves us exposed to some of the problems which the CDC is alleged to have had according to some investigations that have been carried out. We do not think any new agency should be left wide open to those kinds of problems or the possibility of such problems. We think they should be clarified prior to the agency being set up rather than bringing in some doubt as to its ability to function. We do not think that serves either Canagrex, the proposed Crown agency, CDC, or any other Crown agency. Neither does it provide a useful service to farmers to create doubts in the operation because of an inability to explain its business practices to an auditor. We think these items should be spelled out more clearly. We think the minister and some of his officials should appear before the agricultural committee of this House to explain, according to the usual customs and procedures, the bill we will have before us in committee. Generally speaking, as I said at the beginning, we are optimistic about this bill. We think it can have good implications for agriculture, but it must be well managed on the way. Not only must the people who are appointed to this agency do their jobs constructively, but so must members of this House whose function and duty it is to make certain that the bill is as well put together as possible. We think this can only be done in committee and that this bill should not be pushed through the House post-haste.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am most pleased to speak to the House on a bill as important as the one before us tonight, namely an act to establish a Canadian agriculture export corporation, Canagrex. At this point, I want to pay tribute to the farm organizations across Canada and to those farmers who have contributed to the initial discussions of the concept. I want to commend the minister for following their suggestions so closely in the legislation before us tonight.
The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) pointed out that this matter was approved by cabinet almost a year ago. He has perhaps found a little fault on the part of the minister for the delay in bringing this legislation before us. However, I believe the hon. member should look at the number of filibustering delays of last year, particularly last spring. Filibustering took place with regard to the Constitution but also a great deal of time was spent on the Canada lands oil and gas act, which took even more time than the Constitution did. I am not aware that the hon. member had tabled any similar legislation when he was minister, but given a little more time I am sure he would have.
However, I cannot help but respond to his concerns on the funding of this corporation. I can only suggest that one has to walk before one can run. Therefore, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House that in the initial stages we should

January 25, 1982
Canagrex Act
proceed with caution and work with the producers and their organizations to seek out and encourage sales opportunities in areas of highest potential. In this context, Canagrex does not require large amounts of money in its fledgling stages. But surely as the need grows we as a Parliament can make the financial adjustments as required. I for one hope that Canagrex will not result in a large bureaucracy but rather be a slim, trim organization consisting of the best expertise available, acting as a focal point that can work with our farm organizations and marketing boards, the processors and the shippers in a truly Canadian effort that will utilize our technical expertise and, in particular, our potential as outlined in the minister's food strategy report.
In the next few minutes I intend to examine the need for such a body on the basis of the type of agricultural industry which exists in Canada, the problems it is facing in ever-enlarging world markets and the ability of Canagrex to provide a co-ordinated approach to the marketing of our agricultural and food exports.
We all know that the agricultural industry is important to this country's economy. In fact, it is one of the nation's largest employers, and as Canadians we are one of four countries in the world that is a net exporter of food. Canadian farmers, with the population we have, do not have a large enough domestic market to produce only for Canadian use. The export sector is of vital importance to the well-being of Canadian agriculture and of our total economy.
Agriculture exports represent 40 per cent to 44 per cent of total cash farm receipts in Canada while in the United States this percentage is only about 25 per cent. In spite of this, the agriculture industry is not taking full advantage of the market potentials which exist abroad. Agriculture in Canada is characterized by a great diversity of farm products, and in many cases the producers do not have the expertise and the capital to take the risks involved in operating in an international market.
Many federal and provincial government programs lend assistance to agricultural marketing, but none give the necessary comprehensive, co-ordinating assistance which Canagrex will provide that will bring the potential of this industry into proper focus.
We have a challenge to meet here in Canada. At the Canadian agricultural outlook conference held in Ottawa the first week of December of this year, it was projected that the world's population would increase at an annual rate of 1.8 per cent between 1980 and the year 2000, reaching a total of 6.4 billion people by the year 2000. Much of this growth will be in developing countries where 50 cents of every dollar is spent on food. Canagrex will be the vehicle to help Canadian agriculture rise to this growing challenge. Canagrex will provide the opportunity for the Canadian agricultural industry and the diverse marketing infrastructure in place in this country to take advantage of these growing markets. Canagrex will be able to identify and secure markets for producers and to support farmers and their organizations to meet these challenges.
Canagrex will be a co-ordinated marketing effort. It will bring our marketing efforts into focus and will utilize the potential of Canadian farmers and their ability to produce for world markets. Certainly there is a need for close co-operation between the producer, the processor, and the marketing people in order to improve our export markets. We intend to work closely with these groups in an effort to beef up attempts in areas of highest potential.
I am proud to say that the legislation is intended to ensure that farmers and their organizations will be heavily involved in the decision-making process. The proposed policy advisory committee, representing all parts of the food and agriculture sectors, will be appointed by the minister and will meet with the minister to review operations and policies of Canagrex. We also intend Canagrex to work closely with the Canadian Wheat Board and the Canadian Dairy Commission. But in no way is Canagrex intended to duplicate or interfere with any activities or functions of these bodies or simply to become another level of bureaucracy. In fact, it is intended that Canagrex should co-operate fully with existing marketing agencies and boards across Canada. When you examine the situation, you find that we are perhaps the only nation in the world with the capacity to plan our production in an orderly manner so as to meet the terms of long-range contractual agreements and possibly tie selling prices to production costs.
By working in partnership with packers, processors and others in allied industries, we can enter into long-term contractual arrangements which are not as exposed to the vagaries of the marketplace as is the case now, and allow the farmers of Canada to plan production for both domestic and export markets.
Co-ordination is certainly a key word when we talk about Canagrex. There is a need to present foreign buyers with a clearly identifiable institution which deals with all agricultural commodities, except those which are the responsibility of the Canadian Wheat Board and the Canadian Dairy Commission. At present a foreign buyer is sometimes faced with having to deal with as many as 11 governments and their agencies in Canada. The trend is more and more to have governments deal with governments, and Canagrex will provide this facility and avoid the confusion which now faces the foreign buyer. By working with existing marketing agencies, it will work to increase the volume and variety of exports of Canadian agricultural products.
Co-ordination is also needed on the part of those involved in selling our agricultural products abroad. At present, we have ten provincial governments pursuing marketing policies which serve to undercut other provinces. As a consequence, we have producers in one province bidding against those in another, in effect, Canadians bidding against Canadians. An example of this happened several years ago when several provinces, I believe it was five, conducted sales missions to the same country at the same time, all trying to sell pork and bidding against each other. I am aware that last year alone several sales missions were sent abroad by several provinces competing with one another, and certainly that has never made much
January 25, 1982

sense to me. We should be acting as one country selling abroad, not as individual provinces pitted against each other. This will be one possible result of the implementation of this legislation. In addition, I believe the various other problems related to the agricultural industry will also fade or disappear.
It is hoped that we will be able to diversify our exports. Wheat, barley, rapeseed and flaxseed now account for about 60 per cent of Canada's agricultural exports. At the same time Canagrex will be able to foster diversification of markets for agricultural products other than unprocessed grains and oilseeds. Often the United States is the only significant market for other agricultural products. In such a manner Canagrex will be able to co-operate with the producers, processors and marketing institutions at present available in order to increase the volume and variety of sales of our farm products. In this context, I should remind the House that I am aware of several marketing boards which are waiting for the passage of the legislation to assist them in making contracts with other nations who want to deal on a state-to-state basis.
It does not make much sense to me that, in a land with such potential, exports of agricultural products as a percentage of our total exports have declined since 1974. In that year, they accounted for more than 12 per cent of total exports. By 1979-80, they decreased to less than 10 per cent. Certainly this decline exemplifies the need for a co-ordinated approach in marketing abroad.
Canagrex will go a long way toward solving other longstanding agricultural problems faced by the Canadian producer. I have heard a lot of complaints recently from farmers in my area about various things, but one problem in particular surfaced very recently of a buyer who backed out of a contractual arrangement with a private trader, creating a surplus of that product not only here in Canada but a surplus which will eventually reflect back to our neighbours to the south, leaving the producers with a surplus and a bleak year ahead of them as far as this product is concerned. Such an occurrence will be less likely to happen with a Crown corporation dealing on a government to government basis.
In addition, Canagrex will be able to provide bridge financing to assist Third World countries and make export markets less of a risk for the Canadian producer in the sense that another government is less likely to back out of a deal than a private importer. It will also establish the base for long-term contracts which will provide the buyer with continuity of supply of a quality product.
Canadian farmers have the ability, the expertise and the base to produce for these markets. Certainly it is the nature of farmers to want to produce. If you recall Wilkin's law, an economist of the 1930s, we surely must recognize the importance of increased exports of our renewable resources and their contribution to our total economy.
As I indicated earlier, I have talked to scores of farmers and their organizations and I know their reactions. It is our duty as their elected representatives to ensure speedy passage and implementation of this legislation. I know there is a need to find more secure markets, to expand existing markets, and to
Canagrex Act
then encourage production levels to meet those market demands on a continuous basis if we are to take full advantage of the opportunities which will present themselves to the Canadian farmer in the decade ahead.
The goal of Canagrex is to provide new markets to the Canadian producer and to ensure a continuity and stability of income which is not at present available to them. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, if there is an industry in Canada which needs improved marketing capabilities, it has to be agriculture. If there is an industry which needs advice on pricing in the international market, it has to be agriculture. In its present form-and I am not necessarily recommending that form be changed-there is often too little advice on market potential and price on a worldwide basis. This is something which I have advocated ever since I first participated in agricultural organizations, attending Canadian horticultural councils, and ever since I became a member of an elected body, first in the province of New Brunswick and then here.
That advice on and knowledge of the potential of foreign markets has been lacking. I remember, for example, one occasion when I was seeking markets for New Brunswick potatoes as an employee of the government of New Brunswick.
I tried to get a list of potato markets but it was not available from the Department of Agriculture. That was about ten years ago, and that department did not have knowledge of the potato importing countries, nor did it have any knowledge of market prices.
It is for that reason that, when I became a member of the House, I persistently stated that there should be more market information and, as the former minister of agriculture pleaded with the government earlier, there should be consular representation for agriculture on a worldwide basis wherever there may be markets. This is lacking, as the former minister pointed out, and I commend him for his statistics in that regard, and also for pointing out the fact that some of these representatives-at least four of the 11, in my opinion-are located in communities where they can be of little if any value to any aspect of agriculture in the Dominion of Canada. That area has been neglected.
In spite of all the window-dressing which this bill has received and all the promotion which it has been granted, it does not fill the bill. I have several reservations about it.
I think that these reservations are shared by many other people in the agricultural field who have recently spoken. I think it would not be inappropriate to refer to some of their remarks. Mr. Runciman called for an end to production quotas and then added that the Wheat Board should compete with private companies for the farmers' grain instead of having a monopoly over exports of wheat, oats and barley. It is a delusion, he asserted, that a system of planned socialism could be operated according to democratic methods of government.

January 25, 1982
Canagrex Act
He said that a democracy is inseparably linked with capitalism, and that democracy cannot exist under a planned economy. He offered Poland as an example. Farmers must decide whether they are advocates of economic freedom or of socialism. There is no such thing as a little bit of government intervention, said Runciman. A little bit leads to more. He told the farmers in no uncertain terms that they must choose between the market economy and socialism. I agree wholeheartedly with that statement. It is sort of like becoming bald. I do not have a lot of experience, but I am getting there. A few of us become a little bald. The progression is something that we look at with horror after it has begun and over which we have no control. It is with the warning of Mr. Runciman, who has been a long-time agriculturalist, that I speak to the House of Commons and urge caution. Perhaps, if I would not be considered crude, I would say that it is like being a little bit pregnant to introduce a little bit of socialism into this marketing field.
We have also heard a recent statement by the president of the chamber of commerce who, I believe, was once a member of the House on the government side. He, too, has cautioned that we must give the private enterprise system an opportunity to function and that we must not invoke too many regulations and cause too many difficulties to the functioning of our present system.
It is with that in mind that, as I read this bill, I have some concerns. I am concerned that in no place in this bill can I find any point in time at which the committee on agriculture, the committee on public accounts or any other committee will have an opportunity to give an in-depth and analytical look into the operation of Canagrex to determine what it is going to do. It becomes another Crown corporation, one of almost 500 in Canada today, and it does not come under scrutiny in any meaningful way beyond that of the minister and the Auditor General.
1 presume that the minister and hon. members on your right, Mr. Speaker, will say, "But it shall come before a committee of the House for consideration". However, we are in a committee system which gives us a block system. We get an allocation of time. We get a minister of agriculture who fills us with blarney and very little fact at those committee meetings, and time is wasted and information is scarce. I am very concerned that we are creating for agriculture, which is one of the principal interests of my constituency, something which can be swept under the rug. It shall not be accountable to the House of Commons or to the committee on agriculture.
I am further more concerned that Canagrex will also come under government committees, not committees of the House of Commons but committees of ministers. The bill very clearly states that Canagrex will function under the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) but there shall be consultation with other departments of government. There shall be the use of programs of other departments of government. It is not an independent agricultural organization. I am afraid that under these circumstances it will become as subject to extraneous input as would be the farm prices board, which now governs
the egg, poultry and other organizations of Canada, headed by a consumer proponent rather than by an agricultural proponent. That does not give agriculture very much of a chance. We have no assurance, for instance, that the president shall come from the field of agriculture. We have no assurance that the vice-president or the second vice-president, or anyone else, shall be appointed from the active, commercial sector of agriculture.
I am concerned about these things, and I ask the minister, in the pursuit and consideration of this bill, to let us have a better definition than we have at present. I do not want a consumer advocate to be telling agriculture and its marketing processors, "You should not charge more than", as the poultry marketing boards of this nation have been told. The dairy board of this nation has been told, "You shall not use present capital costs as a means of arriving at the cost of producing milk", for instance. There has been an ongoing discussion between the lady chairman of the board and the dairy people and the poultry people concerning the proper costing basis. Will we find ourselves in the same boat under this structure? I must say to Your Honour that if there is to be inflation in the world, then the government, including the Department of Agriculture, must recognize it and govern itself accordingly. We cannot be subject to the whim and pleasure of outside forces if they in turn will not consider the full costs incurred by the agricultural producer.
While I had some favourable thoughts on this bill prior to the time the Minister of Agriculture spoke, I must say that he turned me off when he stated-if I am not quoting him incorrectly, although not absolutely directly-that there are other markets which, for instance, would take the red meats today. He used the American market as an example. He said that we should be able to extract prices from that market which would be profitable to the farmers. The document which I have in my hand indicates that in a week in January, although I am not sure of the exact week, somewhere between 1400 and 1800 head of American cattle arrived on the Canadian market. Why did they come to the Canadian market? It is because they must have received a better return than they could receive in the American market. Can Your Honour tell me how, in the name of the great Father above, the farmer will buy the promotional statement that we could sell meat to the United States because they can afford to buy it at a profit to our farmers when they are already using our market as their market?
Let me give Your Honour another example. The minister said we should be able to sell red meat to the Soviet Union. It was my privilege on one occasion in this House to be part of the House of Commons and Senate committee which was meeting with the European parliamentary delegation. At that particular time, a European parliamentarian told us that approximately 500,000 tonnes of beef were in cold storage because there was no market for it in the European Economic Community. At the same time, there were world news items on that day stating that the Russian agricultural minister, or whatever he might be called-commissioner, commissar-had
January 25, 1982

to reduce the cattle population of Russia because there was not enough grain to feed it. If there had been a market for red meat in Russia, there was lots of red meat to be subsidized by the $10 billion reserve fund of the European Economic Community; yet that meat was lying in cold storage, aging and deteriorating, because there was no market. Let us be reasonable. Had there been a Russian market while they were depleting their herd, the European Economic Community had a $10 billion reserve fund for the subsidization of export of agricultural products surplus to the need of the European Economic Community.
I submit that our Minister of Agriculture has done a great disfavour and a serious disservice to agriculture in Canada by that type of misleading statement. I compliment the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) who supports in principle the idea of Canagrex but who expressed reservations which I hope may become part of the committee process. I hope he will stand as firmly on this and as strenuously as is required in the interests of agriculture. A blind vote for this as it is presently written is not good for agriculture in Canada today or any other day.
The minister talked about selling red meat to Japan. The minister will recall that an element of major progress was made by western pork producers, initiated by the Alberta pork producers. A contract was in fact made to sell pork to Japan. At that time Alberta expanded its hog operations. If my memory serves me correctly, it went to 1,600,000 hogs in Alberta at peak. If I am not mistaken, there are barely 500,000 hogs in Alberta today.
There is no market for any significant amount of pork in Japan. They have been exploring that market for a decade. That is a public body, not government to government as the minister so loudly professes this shall be. However, it is the co-operative structure of Canada dealing with a government in good faith.
While there may be a few more porkers sold there now, certainly the long-term dreams of the pork industry of western Canada have not materialized as a result of a market in Japan. Why? As we passed a red meat act in this House, the Japanese government put in place a control on all meat imports to protect its industry at a level and price which satisfy its farms. The mere passing of this act will not give us what the minister suggests. We may have an agency which can give some information and have some marketing capability, but that is the best we are going to have.
Now, now, don't be so optimistic, Fred.

I will be frank and honest and above board. I am not going to delude farmers into thinking this is the magic wand of price for which they have been looking so long. We already have a price stabilization board and CIDA, both of which should be capable of stimulating exports of our surpluses.
Canagrex Act
The statement has been made that we can control and plan our surpluses. The minister will agree that the present cattle population in Canada will indicate that the price of beef should be good. The present population has gone down very materially. It has not gone down as fast as we would have liked in Argentina, Australia, New Zealand, Brazil or other beef-producing countries. As a result, there is a world market slump in beef.
We cannot plan our beef population in this little country of Canada so that we can cope with world prices unless, as I have said many times, we are prepared to exercise the authority and use the money of the price stabilization board. The population has gone down. However, what the minister overlooks is that so has consumption. The Outlook for Agriculture Conference indicated that not only had the consumption of beef gone down in the last year, it will go down further in the next year.
How can we plan and get rid of those cattle presently walking in the pastures or tied up in the barns so there will not be an excess next year? We cannot predict the economy of this nation. To tell the farmers we can is deceit. To tell the farmers further that we can control world markets and guarantee them prices without price stabilization is further misrepresentation of the facts.
We are doing that with many products now.

Yes, you are. However, if we expand this, we lose our capability to export in the field of agriculture as we lost our capability of exporting in poultry and eggs. We have decimated that export market. We cannot maintain it any better in other fields if we regulate as the minister proposes.
If the Minister of Agriculture were as sincere and believable as he would have us believe, we would have the same incomeaveraging opportunity that the farmers had. We would still have the same depreciation allowance that we had. We would still have the right to sell a farm from father to son. We would not have to pay the capital gains in advance. Where has the minister been?
This is the only country in the world that lets a farmer give a farm to his son tax-free.
That is not correct. Do not mislead the farm population. Farms are inherited and passed on in a dozen countries without any such foolish tax.
There won't be one to pass on. Look at capital gains, capital costs.
They have it in the United States too, remember that.

speechtext:
Order. Usually the Chair can hear the hon. member who has been recognized and is

January 25, 1982
Canagrex Act
standing. We are now hearing from members who are seated and we cannot hear the member who is standing.

Where was the minister when there was an obvious need for bridge financing which is being supplied by other governments? Where is there an organization which will provide money for the farmer on the same basis as some U.S. establishments are doing? When our cattle ranchers and feed-lot operators were paying 20 per cent to 22 per cent, some Americans were paying 8 per cent. Why do we not have anything like that? Where is our bridge financing of 8 per cent? Where has the minister been? Do not deceive the farmers.
Don't you deceive them with your nonsense either.

Where is the minister going to get the expertise to participate in the export market? There are families who have been in the export market for three generations. We are setting up a board with a selection of people without definition of source, including the president, without qualification of expertise or experience in the field of agricultural marketing. If we pass this legislation as it presently exists, we will turn the exporting of agriculture over to the inept and uneducated in that field. Let us get some definition of who will be there.
I suggest to you that the minister does not have any concept of the vast knowledge required to be able to export a single commodity to 50 or 60 countries. I want to know where the expertise comes from when 100 items are exported to as many as 100 countries because I do not want to be part of a House of Commons that passes this responsibility to a group of inept, uneducated and inexperienced individuals.
We have some of the best organizations in Canada, private and governmental.
What is the matter with the Canadian trade service?
They have not been doing it.

I do agree with some of the remarks which were made earlier. I am concerned about the competition that exists among provincial marketing structures. I suggest that these structures are not in the best interests of agriculture. However, the reason that they are competing is that there has not been leadership by this government in combining these structures. The government, through the Minister of Agriculture has had a subsidy plan introduced in British Columbia, Quebec, Ontario, Alberta and Saskatchewan. What will Canagrex be able to do about the price of beef when the oversubsidized Saskatchewan cattle are now going to market and cutting the price received by the farmers who are not subsidized? Why is that, Mr. Speaker? It is because the price
stabilization board is not being used as it historically was and provinces have had to take over in defence of their farmers and replace federal responsibilities. It is misleading for the minister to introduce this legislation as a cure.
We offered them income insurance, 100 per cent of cost of production in 1977. They refused it.
We offered it to them and they said, no way.

Mr. Speaker, they said no because they never dreamed that this government or any other government would completely pull the price stabilization board out of activity and when the price stabilization board proposed an estimate of $300 million in support of the beef industry three or four years ago, it was turned down by the cabinet while he was minister. It never got off the ground.
Because of nothing, Mr. Speaker. Let us not have any more facades. Every member of the House knows that the price stabilization board has been neglected.
Even you know you are wrong in what you are saying.
The price stabilization board policy has been neglected and the minister has been asked to exercise that at 95 per cent by one Canadian organization in agriculture.
They did not want stabilization three years ago.

The minister should show some leadership. The price stabilization that was offered at that time was subject to organization and control of products and marketing. There was a little string attached to it and they would not buy it.
Not at all. We spent more than any government in Canada's history.
On the basis of the inflationary dollar, I doubt if the minister spent 25 cents on the dollar in price stabilization as compared to what was spent by Mr. Gardiner when he was minister.
Fifty cents on the dollar perhaps?
They did not even want that.

They did not want the controls that were brought in by the minister's proposition. The minister knows that as well as does every member in the House. Nothing except at a price.
January 25, 1982
That is nonsense and you know it.

Mr. Speaker, it may be nonsense, but the potato producers of eastern Canada would suggest to you that they have been threatened with no further price stabilization payments if they did not get production and marketing control. They were threatened.
You are saying stabilization is a waste of money when you improve it by better marketing conditions.

I will return to the subject of beef. The most recent publications on beef coming from the government sponsored future of agriculture in December indicated that the consumption was down and would go down further. The minister knows full well that in the beef industry in no way can you anticipate in one year a decline of 2 per cent or 3 per cent. What will be done with the cattle, calves and feeders except to market them? You cannot get rid of them anywhere in the world at this point in time, contrary to what the minister has said. We are not getting the advice which is needed.
If ever an industry needed the publicity of potential prices in the export field, it was the potato industry in the crop year 1981-82. Because that information was not publicized and perhaps not known by the Department of Agriculture, the minister will no doubt use the price cutting of dealers in the world market as an excuse for Canagrex marketing potatoes. If the public had been advised of the potential price in the export market, no sensible dealer could have cut prices to the extent they have been cut this year. That information has not been available and it is needed by the farmers' organizations and those who market. We do not need control of this industry passed over to the government. We do not need the interprovincial competition of marketing boards. We need leadership from the government and a program which will once again try to assume the federal responsibility of agriculture which will remove the interprovincial competition and subsidization which has dislocated certain crops and destroyed the marketing of others.

My first step would never have been to remove the price stabilization board. The removal of that board encouraged the provincial subsidies. The hon. member knows that as well as I do. Someone had to step in to save their farmers and they stepped into a vacuum, starting in British Columbia and Quebec. The hog industry is dislocated. The red beef industry has been dislocated during the minister's tenure in office because there was no leadership and no knowledge of the agricultural industry.
I am not saying that I will not vote for this bill but I do say that in the interest of agriculture we need some responsibility, accountability and an indication where these officers who will run Canada's agricultural industry will come from. At that time let us consider it. In the meantime, we must keep in mind the warning from the member for Humboldt-Lake Centre and

the warning of the former minister. They are real and not imagined.

subtopic: HOUSING-PROJECTED RENTAL INCREASES IN OTTAWA-CARLETON REGION
HOUSING-PROJECTED RENTAL INCREASES IN OTTAWA-CARLETON REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have attended tenants' association meetings in Bayshore in my constituency and I have heard from many tenants in Parkwood Hills and other areas of my riding as well as from other parts of the Ottawa-Carleton area about the situation which has developed and is developing with respect to rental accommodation.
On December 4, 1981, I asked a question of the minister responsible for housing arising out of the budget. The question as it appeared at page 13733 of Hansard was this:
He is aware that in the Ottawa-Carleton region the major rental owner is Minto Management Limited which is intending to raise its rents substantially to some 7,000 to 9,000 tenants. We have one of the lowest vacancy rates in Canada, and there is very little choice in housing in a situation that is virtually a monopoly.
Would the minister please tell the House where in the budget there can be some specific help granted to Ottawa-Carleton so that there can be a choice made in housing? I have looked at the budget. I think the provisions in terms of alternate housing are next to useless. Will the minister make a recommendation to the Minister of Finance that he increase measures for the availability of housing stock so that people will have a choice and not be subject to a monopoly?
In answer to that question this is what the minister said:
Madam Speaker, in the budget announcement dealing with stimulus to rental construction one of the conditions of that housing and its identification for stimulus is that it be located in markets which indeed do have tight vacancy rates. 1 must bring to the attention of the hon. member that the city of Ottawa does not have a tight vacancy rate-
Let the minister tell that to any tenant searching around in the market.
-when compared with other metropolitan areas-
The minister went on to complete his answer.

January 25, 1982
Adjournment Debate
I am not arguing rent control. Rent control is a provincial matter, although I think it is absolutely necessary. It is particularly necessary in a monopoly or a virtual monopoly situation. Rent control is being looked to by the tenants' association, which is active and will be presenting the strongest case possible.
But let me deal with the minister's reasoning, and in the course of my remarks if there is some time, I will want to suggest some policy changes.
The vacancy rate in Ottawa fell from 4.2 per cent in April of 1980 to 0.6 per cent in October of 1981. According to CMHC the Ottawa-Hull area needs 7,800 new units each year. In 1980, only 2,600 new units were built, and data for the first ten months of 1981 suggested that no more than 3,000 new housing units would be built in this area in the year 1981. In other words, less than half the number of required homes and apartments are being built. In the past two years, 9,800 fewer homes were built than were required in the area, and virtually all new rental accommodation over the past few years has been government subsidized.
The major cause of this is high interest rates. At current interest rates it has been estimated that a landlord would have to charge in excess of $800 per month for a one-bedroom apartment in a new building to break even. Until the vacancy rates are either non-existent or until rents rise, private sector builders will not build, given that most people are unwilling to pay that much.
At the same time high interest rates are affecting the ability and the desire of young people to pay $1,000 in monthly mortgage payments. That is not an attractive proposition to a couple paying, for example, $300 in rent. If the couple had purchased a home, their apartment would have been made available to someone else.
The average cost in this area is staggering. In the third quarter of 1981 the average cost of a single family home was $69,000. Assuming a 10 per cent down-payment and 30 per cent of one's income going to principal, interest and tax, a family income of $40,000 a year is needed to afford an average priced home. In terms of meeting this problem this budget is virtually barren of any system by which there can be an attack made on an obvious social condition.

The net effect of the budget is that, instead of rising, the number of housing starts may be reduced. The budget offers builders some assistance for the construction of new homes, up to $7,500 per unit, but in my estimation that would only serve to reduce that $800 a month rent to $700. That is hardly an impact on the situation.
The minister himself has suggested he thinks rent controls should go; that is aside from anything else. I want to tell the minister that is really no policy at all. In that budget MURBs were cancelled when rental accommodation was being built under the MURB provision. This has been replaced with a program of little assistance. The relief for home owners in the
budget is little more than a program that allows people to keep their homes by going further into debt. I know that there is co-operative housing and all these other things; it is one thing to talk about co-operative housing but it is another thing to get it under way.
I believe there should be some major changes in the budget; in fact, the budget should be withdrawn and a new one introduced to provide relief for home owners. This could take the form of subsidized interest rates or mortgage interest deductibility. These measures would be of some help in getting people out of apartments and would encourage them to build homes.
As well, there has to be a recognition of the depth and breadth of the social problem. The reintroduction of MURBs in some form is essential.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think this budget was designed in anticipation of higher rents and, through that system, to give an incentive to landlords to build more units, rather than being a commitment by the federal Liberal Party to help tenants and home owners.
I think the best thing that could be done is to withdraw the budget and to give the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) another chance. Better still, perhaps the government should withdraw the Minister of Finance!

Mr. Speaker, I should like to respond further to the matter raised by the hon. member on December 4 concerning projected rental increases in the Ottawa-Carleton region.
As the hon. member is aware, rental increases in the province of Ontario are governed by provincial legislation. Any increase in rents beyond the provincially established maximum must first receive the approval of the provincial residential tenancy commission. The hon. member is fully aware of that. Rents in Ottawa and elsewhere for a number of years have not been high enough to prompt an adequate rate of new rental construction costs. This has led to a condition of excess demand and it does not surprise me that rental increases are now occurring.
Low vacancy rates prevail in several cities across Canada. As the hon. member knows, apartment vacancy rates in Ottawa declined to 0.9 per cent in October from 2.4 per cent in April of last year. That is a problem. Centres with below 1 per cent vacancy rates are considered to be very tight and to assist these areas the Canada rental supply plan was announced in the budget on November 12. This plan will provide a total of 15,000 rental units across Canada. I wish to assure the hon. member that Ottawa will be included in the allocation of units under this plan. Of course, if the budget were withdrawn that plan would not exist and I am sure the hon. member would not want that to happen. There are, however, areas where the shortage of rental units is more severe.
January 25, 1982

In addition, I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that under the non-profit and co-operative housing programs CMHC will be approving approximately 550 units for low and moderate income families and individuals in the Ottawa area alone during 1982. Mr. Speaker, on November 5 I rose in the House to ask the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) a question regarding the policy within the correctional system of Canada. Specifically I asked whether it was the practice of prison officials to pass on to RCMP officers information regarding criminal conduct of inmates within the penitentiary system whilst they were incarcerated there. I had in mind at that time the career of Clifford Olson. 1 did not want to be specific at the time, partly because 1 wanted to deal with the principle and partly because I did not want to add notoriety to his case and jeopardize the criminal proceedings that had been launched against him.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I was surprised by the answer of the Solicitor General when he told me in the House on that day that it was indeed the practice of prison officials to pass information on to RCMP officers regarding criminal activity within the prison system.
I have checked on matters before and after that occasion and while I have no specific documentation, it is my clear understanding that RCMP officers are not privy to information regarding criminal activity engaged in by inmates within the prison system. The RCMP do not get that documented information. They must rely on street talk, particularly, and the gossip within that subculture of the prison population.
There are some people who believe that Mr. Olson would have been apprehended sooner had the RCMP known of his behaviour while he was an inmate at the B.C. Penitentiary. Specifically, as a result of Mr. Olson's behaviour prior to 1977 and 1978, was his name on a sex offender list held by the RCMP? Had he been on that list, would that not possibly have helped the RCMP to have apprehended him sooner?
I am sure the Solicitor General knows that in early 1976 Clifford Olson raped a young man at the B.C. Penitentiary. I am sure the Solicitor General knows the young man in question. Right after that three inmates in the protective custody unit attacked Clifford Olson. While that attack was being engaged in, there were over 75 inmates in the PCU at the B.C. Penitentiary watching. This was unprecedented at the B.C. Penitentiary, and the officials there knew that something had to be done. Thus, almost immediately they transferred him to Prince Albert where he was immediately attacked and stabbed by three inmates. It was as a result of that attack that he was awarded $3,500 by the Saskatchewan Crimes Compensation Board, which in its award noted that his conduct was above
Adjournment Debate
reproach, that he indicated an unusual degree of moral and physical courage and that he underwent a great deal of emotional turmoil. In June, 1977, Mr. Olson was back at the B.C. Penitentiary. He was the key witness in the trial of one Gary Marcoux, another man arrested and charged with a sex offence and murder. It is clear that without the testimony of Clifford Olson at that trial Marcoux could not-and I underscore "could not" have been convicted.
Did the penitentiary officials at the B.C. Penitentiary scrub Mr. Olson's files so that he would appear to be a credible witness at the Gary Marcoux trial? The Solicitor General will know that within that trial there was a very lengthy voir dire which dealt with the admissibility of evidence, and that evidence concerned the correspondence between Olson and Marcoux; something like 100 pages of correspondence. Would the judge at that voir dire have accepted the testimony of Mr. Olson had the judge known the career of Clifford Olson in the B.C. Penitentiary prior to the arrest and trial of Gary Marcoux? Why was the Crown prosecutor who used Mr. Olson at that trial so solicitous in helping him after the trial was over? I have a letter written by the Crown prosecutor to the chairman of the National Parole Board. In it, in part, he said:
I have no hesitation in saying that Marcoux would have gone free but for the evidence that Olson gathered and to which he testified during the course of the trial. Marcoux is a dangerous sex offender and should not, in the writer's opinion, be allowed in our community and I, as a citizen of this country, am grateful to Mr. Olson for assisting the Crown in convicting this man.
I should like to know why the prosecutor, who just last month or earlier this month became defense counsel for Mr. Olson and was previously the Crown prosecutor using Mr. Olson in the trial of Gary Marcoux, was so solicitous in helping Mr. Olson by writing to the chairman of the National Parole Board. Could it be that even the Crown prosecutor was not privy to the career of Mr. Olson while he was an inmate at the B.C. penitentiary? Did he know that Clifford Olson had raped someone, that he had been attacked by other members of the protective custody unit within the B.C. penitentiary and in Prince Albert because of that attack on a young man at the B.C. penitentiary? These are very serious questions. Underlying them is whether or not there is collusion among the officials of the correctional system to protect certain inmates and clean up their files so they will appear to be better inmates in the eyes of certain officials in the future.

Mr. Speaker, for some months now the hon. member has been raising this general question about the extent to which the correctional service of Canada warns the police and municipalities to which offenders are being returned about their criminal records. The hon. member has not until tonight indicated that he was specifically interested in any particular offender. He tells me tonight that the offender in which he is interested is Clifford Olson and the trial about which he has a number of specific questions is not the Olson trial but the Marcoux trial. Indeed, I will look into all of these questions and do the best I can to

January 25, 1982
Adjournment Debate
furnish answers, bearing in mind that provincial court records are not within my jurisdiction.
Nevertheless, the questions which the hon. member asked are interesting and I am anxious to get to the bottom of them. However, I want to remind the hon. member, because it is sometimes contradicted in the media, that Clifford Olson at the time of the series of murders for which he was recently convicted was not a parolee. He was not under mandatory supervision. He was free because his warrant justifying his incarceration and justifying mandatory supervision had expired. He was free to go anywhere in Canada without reporting to the police or without reporting to members of the parole service or the correctional service of Canada. The kind of authority which the correctional service has over a person after his or her warrant has expired is much more limited.
I want to assure the hon. member, and through him the people of British Columbia, that the correctional service of Canada and the RCMP are far from being two solitudes and, whatever existed historically, there presently is a very close relationship not only with the RCMP but with all the police forces in Canada. In fact, my ministry originally sponsored a very successful joint committee, which is a national committee, bringing together senior officials of the correctional service of Canada and senior members of the police community. But there are also regional divisions of that organization. I believe over 40 meetings were held last year in the regions. One of the main purposes of these meetings is to exchange information about dangerous individuals known to the correctional service of Canada.
In addition to that, as I have indicated in answers to the House, the correctional service of Canada does provide information about offenders who are going into a community. Prison records are provided and telephone calls are made in serious cases to alert the police of the risk of an offender who is known to be dangerous, who was incarcerated and who is returning to a particular community. That is not only customary for the RCMP, but for all police forces. It does not do a service to criminal justice for the hon. member to create the impression that we are talking here about the old system of two solitudes where the correctional service never took any interest in people once they were back on the street. That is no longer the case.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO PAYMENT MADE TO CONVICTED MURDERER, CLIFFORD OLSON SUGGESTED RECOVERY OF FUNDS
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO PAYMENT MADE TO CONVICTED MURDERER, CLIFFORD OLSON SUGGESTED RECOVERY OF FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today during the course of question period I raised certain serious questions with the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) concerning the Clifford Olson case, questions which are being asked by many thousands of Canadians from coast to coast about this black day in Canadian legal history.
I called upon the Solicitor General to order a full independent public inquiry into the circumstances of this payment and the manner in which the investigation was conducted. In addition, I urged the Solicitor General to make a very clear,
unequivocal statement in this House that never again in Canadian history would he, as Solicitor General, or his successors, authorize the payment of such blood money to a person suspected or accused of committing a crime, especially the most serious crime which can be committed in Canadian society, that is the taking of another person's life.
Since the announcement of this payment during the course of the trial of Clifford Olson and the announcement of the nature of the investigation and some of the questions raised about that investigation, the B.C. Attorney General, Allan Williams, was caught in a barefaced lie. The Solicitor General himself has made a number of blatantly contradictory statements.
At one point he said that he had the power to veto the payments made to the family of Clifford Olson. He indicated he was informed shortly after the decision was made; there was a reference at one point to "a couple of days". In any event, there was a clear statement that he had veto power over this decision.
However, it now turns out he was not informed until more than two weeks after the decision to authorize payments was in fact made, and after payments were made to the trust fund. How can he possibly suggest that at that point he could have vetoed this particular decision? He has said there was a convictable case at the point at which the decision was made to authorize payment. However, that evidence has been disputed not only by the B.C. attorney general, but also by the commissioner of the RCMP.
In addition, the Solicitor General will know as a lawyer that any evidence obtained either through fear of punishment or hope of reward would certainly be thrown out of court. That is a cardinal principle of our criminal law, and is confirmed in the charter of rights.
The Solicitor General indicated at one point that no federal money was paid to the family of Clifford Olson. He then said the federal amount was 44 per cent, which then became 75 per cent. In fact, Mr. Speaker, every penny of this money must be paid by the federal government under the terms of the contract between it and the province of British Columbia. Section 14 of that contract states very clearly that any ex gratia payments must be paid in full by the federal government.
What does the Solicitor General say in a classic case of buck passing? He says it is not his responsibility. He wants to leave it to the attorney general of British Columbia. The fact of the matter is that it was his responsibility to make the decision to authorize payment. Those funds are coming out of the federal treasury and it is, indeed, his responsibility under the RCMP Act to ensure that a major decision such as this is only taken with the consent of the federal Solicitor General.
There is a second aspect to this case which warrants investigation. I called upon the Solicitor General to assure Canadians that a payment such as that made to Clifford Olson would never be made again under similar circumstances, and that this should not be allowed to establish a precedent. There is a

fundamental rule in Canadian law that a criminal must not be allowed to profit from his crimes. This rule has been violated and a very dangerous precedent has been set. Twisted minds may decide to kill for profit. Others may be induced to confess to crimes they did not commit.
All of us understand the anguish that the parents felt in these circumstances. I am a member from British Columbia and I know the pressure on the police, but this kind of payment cannot be tolerated. I was approached by the parents of one of the murdered children who asked me why that man was able to profit from the death of their child?
Other questions must be raised in the course of an inquiry about the nature of this investigation. Why was Clifford Olson not under detailed and intensive surveillance from the moment he became a prime suspect on July 15, 1981? In view of his record and in view of the fact that he was a prime suspect, why was he not under the most intensive form of surveillance? Inspector Proke says, frankly, he cannot tell why the delay occurred. Other questions have been raised. Was Olson on the RCMP payroll at any point as an informer? Was there an accomplice working with Olson on some of these murders? Why was this man not behind bars in view of certain charges made against him and in view of his lengthy record. There are many questions which remain unanswered in the Clifford Olson saga, such as the circumstances of the payment and the manner in which the investigation was handled.
1 would very seriously suggest that if the Solicitor General does not respond to this strong outcry by Canadians from coast to coast and order a public inquiry to settle some of these serious questions, he will bring the office of the Solicitor General into disrepute and he will have no alternative but to resign forthwith.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-REQUEST FOR INQUIRY INTO PAYMENT MADE TO CONVICTED MURDERER, CLIFFORD OLSON SUGGESTED RECOVERY OF FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has added very little to the questions which he raised in the House this afternoon during question period. I think I gave my answers to those questions at that time. I want to take advantage of the opportunity, however, to indicate why I think a public inquiry into the police investigation would be highly undesirable.
There were three or four prime suspects who were being watched by the police, and there were a great many other people who had accusations brought against them. If there were to be a public inquiry, the public would have to be informed as to who those other suspects were and what the evidence was against them, which was false evidence in some cases, and how the police weighed that evidence in making a decision as to whether it was Olson or whether it was them.
Adjournment Debate
One might say that we could bring the evidence forward but leave out the names of the suspect. However, if one leaves the names out and includes their addresses, places of business, and associates, which were all very important in assessing their possible responsibility in the matter, they would be identified. I think it would be extremely unfair to the other suspects of these murders, who were cleared when Olson was convicted, to bring forward the cases against them which led the police to consider them to be suspects.
If one wanted to assess how the police were doing, and why, until they charged Olson, they thought he might either be guilty or innocent, one would have to know what they thought they had against the other people. One would have to name them or give their names and addresses, which would amount to the same thing, in order to make it possible to review the judgment that the police were exercising in the case.
Then one would have to involve the parents of many, many children in the area where these crimes were committed, those parents who came forward and told the police their children had been the victims of sexual assaults of one kind or another. One would have to give their names in order that the public inquiry could understand why their evidence was important; or, if one left their names out, one would have to give their addresses or something of their descriptions, such as where they worked and how it was that these four suspects and others who were accused came into contact with them.
I think when one indicates what happens when a police report is made public, it is obvious why it should not be made public. If the parents of a child who was a victim or thought to be a victim of a sexual offence came to the police, knowing that in the following few weeks the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) would have the right to have that information made public and broadcast across the country, even if their names, their address and their places of work were omitted, what kind of public inquiry could we have?
This is a case where the attorney general of a province and the Solicitor General of Canada share a responsibility. Their duties are different, but they have this responsibility because it would be unfair and wrong, as well as disruptive and destructive of police operations, for inquiries of this sort to be made public. I think police work would be very seriously deteriorated if this information was made public, even with names and identifications expurgated to avoid prejudice. This just would not mean anything to anyone who wanted to assess it.
